## Introduction 
We've previously talked about the [benefits of continuous integration](continuous-integration.qmd) and [test matrices development](test-matrix.qmd). This blog article focuses on setting up continuous integration of high performance resources locally, instead of using a paid hosting option such as Github's or Gitlab's "runners".

>[!caution]
>Before implementing automated testing, it is important to acknowledge that there are security implications whenever new and untrusted or unverified code is executed locally. 
>  - The testing system can be set up to automatically pull from a repository, meaning that anyone with write access can execute code on the test device. Managing permissions of the test user, and limiting access to resources may be required, in addition to controlling write access to the repository or branches with automated testing.
    - In shared environments (like most HPC clusters), denial of resources is possible with incorrect or malicious jobs. For instance, an incorrectly set partition could result in a series of tests overwhelming a specific hardware resource. Testing timeouts may be necessary.

This blogpost contains ideas and concepts from a variety of sources, including but not limited to:
 - The User Manuals for [Jenkins](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/), [Singularity](https://singularityhub.github.io/), [Github Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions), [Gitlab CI/CD](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/), [Spack](https://spack.io/), [NVIDIA Container Toolkit](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit), [Docker](https://www.docker.com/), [Slurm Workload manager](https://slurm.schedmd.com/overview.html)
 - Open Access articles including [Continuous Integration and Delivery for HPC: Using Singularity and Jenkins, Zebula Sampedro](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3219104.3219147)
 - Event presentations, including [Building an efficient Continuous Integration workflow on HPC systems, RSECon 2024 - Tobias Ribizel](https://zenodo.org/records/14290374)
 - Blog Articles from the wider software engineering community, including those by [Martin Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/articles/continuousIntegration.html#StylesOfIntegration)

## Self hosted vs off premises hosting
The two options for hosting automated CI workflows are hosting a server, and paying someone to host a server for you. While it would appear that self hosting is the cheaper option, it is important that any funding streams, such as grant applications, take into account additional workload for System Administrators, additional hardware usage or procurement, and the possibility of downtime.
Reasons to self host:
  - Hardware resources or software environments can't be fulfilled by major hosting companies offerings. With special reference to High Performance Computing applications, the requirements to fully test a program, or a parallelisation strategy, may require substantially more compute than can feasibly be purchased from major providers such as Gitlab and Github. In addition, the heterogeneous nature of the compute required can prevent a particular configuration from being requested at all·
  - More customisable, customisation must be documented.
Reasons use off premises hosting:
  - Fast to set up
  - Documentation available, customisation must be documented
  - Relatively fixed costs
  - Separate pool of resources for compute vs testing
  - Reduced security implications from poorly formulated program versions.
  - Available from anywhere with an internet connection.

## Walkthrough
### SHAREing internal
The structure of SHAREing's development at Durham is centralised on Github. Github organises continuous integration into Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD). 
The Github hosted build and test schema is called Github Actions. These are user defined or community maintained configurations which instruct a Github-hosted "Runner" ( a lightweight Linux, MacOS or Windows instance as detailed in the [Github Documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners#supported-runners-and-hardware-resources) ). These configurations are defined in a Github flavoured dialect of YAML and are stored in a ` .github/workflows ` directory. These actions allow for the specification of a build and test matrix which can be triggered on certain Github events, such as pushes to a particular branch, or as part of pull requests. The matrix defines every combination of build condition and test, such that any particular build of a commit is tested completely. For example, a build stage may toggle support of the Message Passing Interface Standard, so it is important that the test suite tests both the version of the build with this capability, and the one without.
